To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the inferior parietals, the left middle temporal gyrus, and the left superior temporal gyrus are activated when verbs with multiple obligatory arguments are compared with verbs with a single obligatory argument.
the inferior parietals are engaged for processing verb argument structure, with increasing activation in these regions associated with increased argument structure complexity.

argument structure complexity, as measured by the number of obligatory arguments associated with verbs, is associated with activation of the supraparietal region, with bilateral activation noted for the comparison of two- versus one-argument verbs and left-lateralized activation for the comparison of verbs with two versus one argument.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain processes language.
the neural instantiation of verb argument structure complexity and the relationship of these processes to semantic integration.
the neural correlates of the processing of verbs by argument-structure complexity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
verbs and nouns are processed similarly in the brain.
verbs and nouns are processed in similar brain regions and that argument structure processing is reflected in increased activation in posterior peri-sylvia regions.
the neural instantiation of verb processing is associated with the integration of semantic and syntactic information, with the posterior peri-sylvan regions playing a key role in such integration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural instantiation of verb argument structure complexity involves the supramarginals and angular gyri bilaterally, with increasing activation associated with increasing argument complexity.
the brain regions that are involved in processing verbs are the same ones that are involved in the processing of nouns.
the neural instantiation of the verb argument structure is not a unitary process but instead is dependent on the argument structure complexity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the brain is a very powerful tool to investigate the neural correlates of language processing, and that it is possible to investigate the neural mechanisms that underlie language processing using functional magnetic resonance imaging.
the brain is not only capable of representing the meaning of words, but that it can represent different kinds of words in similar ways.
the brain is not a general purpose computer, but rather a highly specialized device that has evolved to perform a variety of complex tasks.
